ALEX: Alright. The No Kings Coalition — an anti-Trump group organizing early voting for the November midterms — had their Instagram account suspended Saturday afternoon for about ninety minutes. And when Meta explained why, they pointed at a Claude-based AI tool. So what actually happened?
JAMIE: The tool was scraping Instagram — reading profiles, posts, hashtags — but doing it at four times the speed of a normal human browsing the site. Meta's automated security systems saw that pattern and said: bot. Account suspended.
ALEX: So the tool wasn't trying to hurt the coalition. It was associated with them somehow?
JAMIE: That's the thing Meta still hasn't answered. They haven't said who was operating the tool, or why it was connected to that account. They just said: this is what the traffic looked like, this is what triggered it.
RUFUS: Which is where it gets interesting, technically. The security system doesn't ask why the traffic is fast. It only sees that it is. Intent is invisible to the classifier.
ALEX: So "bot" now just means anything that moves faster than a person.
RUFUS: Essentially. It's a behavioral category, not a moral one.
JAMIE: Right, and that's the part that should bother people beyond the tech explanation. Because the account went down during active election-period protests. Ninety minutes during a get-out-the-vote push isn't nothing.
ALEX: And Meta said sorry, restored it, but admin access was delayed even longer.
JAMIE: Several additional hours, yes.
ALEX: Okay but I want to push on something. There's a version of this where Meta's system is actually working correctly. It saw non-human traffic at abnormal speed and acted on it. That's the system doing its job.
RUFUS: It is. That's not in dispute. The question is whether "working correctly" is sufficient when you can't distinguish between a legitimate AI agent that a coalition is using for monitoring, and a malicious bot attack designed to look identical.
JAMIE: Because from the outside they look exactly the same. Four-times-speed burst traffic is four-times-speed burst traffic. The packet doesn't carry a note saying "we're the good guys."
ALEX: So who's on the hook here? Meta? The Claude tool operator? Anthropic?
RUFUS: Meta hasn't identified the operator. They haven't identified the specific tool. So there's no clear chain of responsibility published.
JAMIE: Which is also a convenient position to be in when the suspension is drawing censorship accusations.
ALEX: You think Meta is using the AI explanation as cover?
JAMIE: I think "a Claude AI tool did it" is a cleaner answer than "our systems suppressed a political group during an election." Whether that's intentional framing or just accurate reporting, I genuinely don't know. But they haven't given us enough to rule either out.
RUFUS: The detail that's missing is the most important one. Why was this particular tool interacting with this particular account?
ALEX: And we just don't know.
RUFUS: Meta says they don't know. Or they haven't said what they know.
JAMIE: Those are different things.
RUFUS: Yes they are.
ALEX: Okay here's the part that's actually actionable for anyone listening who uses AI tools for social monitoring — which is a lot of organizations now. What does this mean for them?
JAMIE: It means the platform's security system doesn't care about your intentions. If you're running an agent that scrapes or monitors social media, and it's making requests in bursts at speeds no human could produce, you are at risk of looking like a bot attack. Because you are, technically, producing bot-like traffic.
RUFUS: The practical fix is rate limiting. You throttle how fast the tool makes requests so it stays within a range that reads as plausibly human.
ALEX: Caffeinated human, maybe. Not four-times-normal-speed human.
RUFUS: Precisely. A caffeinated human, not a caffeinated teenager on deadline.
JAMIE: And the broader thing to watch is that this is only going to get more common. More organizations are deploying agents that interact with platforms. Platform security systems are getting more sensitive because actual bot attacks are also getting more sophisticated. These two curves are on a collision course.
ALEX: We've been asking on the show who's responsible when an AI agent makes an error at work. This is kind of a live example.
JAMIE: It really is. And the answer so far is: whoever you can least easily hold accountable.
RUFUS: Which in this case is an unnamed operator of an unidentified tool.
ALEX: Perfect.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our second story is a good one. MIT researchers have published work on a multimodal AI — and I'll explain what that means in a second — that can help discover new materials. Jamie, this is the story you actually lit up about when we were prepping.
JAMIE: I did, because it's the kind of thing AI is genuinely well-suited to that most people don't hear about. So: multimodal means the system is working with more than one type of input at the same time. Most AI models we talk about are text-in, text-out. This one takes 3D atomic crystal structures and natural language descriptions and uses them together.
ALEX: So it's reading a scientific paper about a material and also seeing the actual atomic arrangement?
JAMIE: Exactly. Think about the problem they're solving. You've got huge databases of 3D crystal structures from computational chemistry. Separately, you've got decades of scientific literature describing what materials do, how they behave, what they're good for. Those two bodies of knowledge basically don't talk to each other.
ALEX: Because one is visual-structural and one is text.
JAMIE: Right. A materials scientist trying to find a new battery electrolyte has to mentally bridge those two worlds. This model learns to bridge them automatically, using something called contrastive learning.
ALEX: Which means what, exactly?
JAMIE: Contrastive learning — in plain terms — is a training method where you teach the model that "this structure" and "this description" go together, and "that structure" and that other description do not go together. You're training it on matching pairs. Over time it learns a shared language between the atomic picture and the prose.
RUFUS: It's a bit like teaching someone to recognize wine by pairing the taste with vocabulary, rather than teaching the vocabulary and the taste separately.
JAMIE: That's actually a good analogy.
RUFUS: I have them occasionally.
ALEX: Don't tell him that, he'll become insufferable.
RUFUS: I already was.
ALEX: So what did the model actually demonstrate it could do better?
JAMIE: Identifying crystals suited for solid-state lithium-ion batteries. Solid-state batteries are the big prize in green energy storage — they're safer, potentially more energy-dense than the liquid electrolyte batteries in most devices now. Finding the right materials for them is a massive research bottleneck.
ALEX: And AI is saying: I can read through the atomic database and the literature simultaneously and flag candidates faster.
JAMIE: Much faster. Though — and this is the qualifier that matters — the paper appeared in Nature Communications in August. What MIT released this week is the public announcement. The lab results still need experimental validation.
RUFUS: Which is a gap worth keeping in mind. Rufus, take us on location.
ALEX: Rufus, take us on location.
RUFUS: Right. So the source reporting here is from MIT, no specific geographic location for the research that would put me usefully anywhere. So consider this the global desk perspective.
JAMIE: But the timeline to an actual commercial battery from a research paper is still measured in years, not months.
RUFUS: It is. The honest version of this is: the model is a better prospector. It narrows the field of candidates for human researchers and experimental validation to pursue. It doesn't replace the experiments.
ALEX: Back to the wider story. So the honest claim is this accelerates discovery, not that it completes it.
JAMIE: Which is still meaningful. Drug discovery, materials science — these fields spend enormous time and money on the candidate identification phase. Shortening that phase is real progress even if everything after it looks the same.
ALEX: You said earlier that Rufus found an AI use he actually likes. Is that true?
RUFUS: I find this more legible than most. The problem is specific. The method has a mechanistic explanation. The application is testable. I prefer that to announcements that an AI has become "more helpful."
JAMIE: He's not wrong about that.
ALEX: I know, it's annoying. What should listeners watch for?
JAMIE: Materials science journals. If this model is functioning as claimed, you'd expect to see follow-up papers from MIT or collaborators reporting experimental results on specific crystal candidates for battery electrolytes. That's the signal that the research is translating.
RUFUS: And if the paper from August generates no experimental follow-up, that's also informative.
ALEX: In the less encouraging direction.
RUFUS: Correct.
JAMIE: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Alex, if everything is breaking news, when are we supposed to get any work done?
ALEX: That's the question The Ledger helps you work through: five focused briefings connecting AI news with the decisions in front of you.
RUFUS: The Ledger. Because reading another headline is a marvellous way to postpone deciding anything. I admire the efficiency of the procrastination.
JAMIE: Rufus has diagnosed the problem. The Ledger link is in our show notes. Back to the story.

scenes.original:
ALEX: Our third story. Anthropic this week announced a Public Benefit Fund. They're committing five percent of their shares to it. And there's a scaling mechanism built in — an additional two percent of shares for every fifty percent increase in the company's value. Rufus, you want to explain the structure before Jamie and I ask uncomfortable questions about it?
RUFUS: Gladly. The fund is structured as a wholly-owned LLC — a limited liability company. Not a foundation, not a 501(c)(3) charity. Wholly owned means it's Anthropic's LLC, which means Anthropic retains control over it. The equity — the five percent of shares — cannot be used for lobbying or political contributions. That's explicitly prohibited.
ALEX: And it's subject to stockholder approval.
RUFUS: Which hasn't happened yet.
JAMIE: So it's a commitment pending approval to a fund they own, to do public benefit work they haven't yet specified the governance of.
RUFUS: The governance details are described as forthcoming.
JAMIE: Right. And they've also previously committed two hundred million dollars to study AI's economic effects. So this is in addition to that.
ALEX: What's the stated purpose?
RUFUS: Addressing labor market impacts of AI is the example given. So: AI displacing workers, essentially.
ALEX: Okay. I want to take this seriously for a moment, because there are two very different ways to read it. One is: this is a company that's building technology that could significantly disrupt labor markets, and they're setting aside equity that scales with their own value to address that. That's structurally interesting.
JAMIE: It is structurally interesting. The tiered model is actually novel. As Anthropic gets more valuable, more equity goes to the fund. So the obligation grows with the impact, theoretically.
RUFUS: Theoretically. The two percent trigger is at the board's discretion.
JAMIE: Which is where my skepticism lives. The board decides when to add the next two percent. The governance of the fund itself hasn't been published. Who decides what counts as a public benefit initiative? Anthropic, currently.
ALEX: Is there any precedent for this kind of structure that actually worked?
RUFUS: There are precedents for corporate foundations with equity stakes. Some have independent governance that functions well. Some are marketing exercises with charitable tax status. The difference is usually whether there's external oversight with real decision-making power.
JAMIE: And we don't know yet which this is.
RUFUS: We don't. Anthropic says governance details are coming in the next few months. That's the thing to wait for.
ALEX: Jamie, you used the phrase "corporate conscience tax" in prep. Make the case.
JAMIE: The case is: if you're building the thing that might eliminate a category of jobs, setting aside five percent of your equity for a fund you control to study the problem is a way of appearing to address it without actually being accountable to anyone outside the company. The LLC structure is the tell. If you wanted genuine independence, you'd set up a foundation with an independent board.
RUFUS: That's a fair criticism of the current structure. It's also incomplete, because the governance details haven't been published.
JAMIE: Right, which is exactly the problem. We're being asked to evaluate an accountability mechanism without the accountability details.
ALEX: Rufus, you said in prep you think this is a pragmatic step forward. Defend that.
RUFUS: The equity-scaling model is genuinely novel. Most corporate social responsibility commitments are fixed amounts that become proportionally smaller as the company grows. This one explicitly grows with the company's value. If Anthropic's valuation doubles, more shares flow to the fund. That alignment, if it holds, is more honest than a one-time donation.
JAMIE: If it holds. "At the board's discretion" is a very large caveat.
RUFUS: It is. But so is "pending governance details" being a reason to dismiss it before they're published.
ALEX: Is there a version of this where you're both right?
JAMIE: The structure has real potential and the current safeguards are insufficient.
RUFUS: That's essentially my position.
JAMIE: Then why are we arguing?
RUFUS: Force of habit.
ALEX: What's the practical thing for people to watch?
RUFUS: The governance disclosure. Anthropic has said it's coming in the next few months. The specific questions are: does the fund have an independent board, does that board have genuine spending authority, and what are the criteria for what qualifies as a public benefit initiative.
ALEX: If the answer to all three is yes, it's meaningful. If the answer is that Anthropic decides everything—
JAMIE: Then it's a well-designed press release.
RUFUS: With a financial mechanism that's better than most press releases.
JAMIE: I'll give it that.
